Energy Department Closes $480 Million Loan to Expand American Energy Production and Strengthen Offshore Infrastructure in the Gulf of America
WASHINGTON—The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) today announced the financial close of a $480 million loan for Arena Energy's Project Elkhorn to increase oil and natural gas production across the Gulf of America shelf. The project will modernize 22 offshore platforms off the coast of Louisiana and, at peak production, is expected to add up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day and up to 77 million cubic feet of natural gas per day to U.S. energy production.
Today’s announcement is made possible by President Trump’s Working Families Tax Cut and marks the Energy Department's first closed loan supporting domestic oil and natural gas production, underscoring DOE’s commitment to advancing American energy dominance and delivering affordable, reliable, and secure energy for American families and businesses.
“The United States is the world’s largest producer and exporter of oil and natural gas, and thanks to President Trump, American energy production will continue to grow,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs. By providing financing for projects like Project Elkhorn, the Energy Department is expanding domestic production and strengthening our energy security to power American prosperity for decades to come.”
Arena Energy currently produces approximately 30,000 barrels of oil per day offshore in the Gulf of America. Project Elkhorn will modernize existing offshore infrastructure and expand production capacity—adding approximately 125 million barrels of oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas to U.S. energy production over the life of the project. The project will create 2,400 construction-related jobs and 400 operations jobs in one of the nation's most important offshore energy corridors.
“Thanks to President Trump and Secretary Wright’s leadership, EDF is putting existing energy infrastructure back to work for the American people,” said EDF Director Gregory A. Beard. “Project Elkhorn will expand domestic oil and natural gas production, create good-paying American jobs, and strengthen our energy security while generating substantial returns for American taxpayers.”
Under President Trump’s leadership, EDF is financing American energy infrastructure projects that increase domestic production, strengthen U.S. energy security, and lower costs for all Americans while responsibly managing taxpayer dollars.

"BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm–System Co-Design

DaYou Du1,  Woon Yee Ng1,  Guangming Sheng2,  Nick Lau2,  Jianyi Cheng1,  Luo Mai1
1University of Edinburgh  2Tencent Hunyuan

🖂 dayou.du@ed.ac.uk

Abstract

The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm–system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4–3.0× higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://t.co/t3Hqg3otzo.
1Introduction
Modern large language models (LLMs) have rapidly expanded their context windows, with recent frontier models supporting up to 1M tokens (Gemini Team et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), enabling complex applications such as long-document comprehension, repository-level coding, and test-time reasoning scaling (Wei et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025). However, serving these models at long contexts and large batch sizes is severely bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache (Kwon et al., 2023; Du et al., 2026). Unlike static model weights, the KV cache grows linearly with both sequence length and concurrency, quickly dominating GPU memory capacity and bandwidth as it is repeatedly loaded during decoding (Xia et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026).Quantizing the KV cache to low precision effectively compresses its memory footprint and reduces data movement (Liu et al., 2024; Hooper et al., 2024). Recently, 4-bit microscaling formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4 (Rouhani et al., 2023; NVIDIA, 2025c) have improved low-bit numerical fidelity while enabling native 4-bit matrix multiplications directly on Tensor Cores, delivering 2× or higher throughput than FP8 on modern NVIDIA Blackwell and Rubin GPUs (NVIDIA, 2025a) and eliminating the runtime dequantization overhead of low-bit KV caches. Recent works further show that these formats achieve high accuracy and efficiency for weight and activation quantization in training and inference (Cook et al., 2025; Egiazarian et al., 2026), as well as for prefill and non-causal attention (Zhang et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026).However, for autoregressive KV cache decoding, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration, as shown in Figure 1 (right). On the one hand, existing efficient NVFP4 KV cache systems such as TRT-LLM-NVFP4 (NVIDIA, 2025d) directly apply vanilla NVFP4 to the KV cache, causing severe accuracy drops in long-context inference; meanwhile, DeepInfer (DeepSeek-AI, 2026b; DeepSeek-AI, 2026a) relies on post-training without considering the underlying quantization error. On the other hand, accuracy-oriented KV quantization algorithms such as TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2026) rely on vector codebooks whose online lookup and reconstruction overhead is inefficient on GPUs, severely degrading decoding https://t.co/LlqP3JiEq0 further push decoding performance, executing attention natively on FP4 Tensor Cores while preserving accuracy poses coupled algorithmic and system challenges. First, at the algorithm level, whereas dequantization-based kernels keep queries Q and softmax probabilities P in 16 or 8 bits, native FP4 attention requires all four operands (Q,K,P,V) in narrow 4-bit microscaling blocks. During long-context decoding, query rounding noise is broadcast across thousands of tokens, small probabilities P severely underflow under 8-bit E4M3 block scales, and token-wise Tensor Core block layouts clash with steep channel-wise outliers in K. Second, at the system level, simply invoking FP4 Tensor Cores on paged KV caches (Kwon et al., 2023; Du et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026) does not automatically yield decoding speedups: as matrix multiplication accelerates, the bottleneck shifts to CUDA-core softmax reductions, and accuracy-preserving quantization steps (e.g., per-tile FP32 rescaling or extra query GEMMs (Zhang et al., 2025b)) stall the decoding pipeline if not co-designed with the kernel.Figure 1:Overview of BitDecoding-FP4 (left), achieving higher accuracy and serving throughput when running Qwen3-4B (right). See Table 1 for the average accuracy and Figure 10(b) for the per-GPU serving throughput on B300 at 128K context.
In this paper, we present BitDecoding-FP4, which addresses both challenges through an algorithm–system co-design for native FP4 KV cache decoding, as illustrated in Figure 1 (left). At the algorithm level, we identify and mitigate the three primary error sources in native FP4 attention: (i) Dual-Residual Query Quantization represents the query as the sum of two FP4 tensors to suppress logit error from query quantization; (ii) Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 block scales from rounding small long-context softmax probabilities to zero via exponent rescaling and adaptive scale-maximum selection; and (iii) Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static key smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and block-scale search to tame key channel outliers under token-wise quantization. At the kernel level, we remove the softmax bottleneck with a transposed softmax that parallelizes reductions across keys and fuses probability quantization into warp-level butterfly shuffles, while stacked query MMA folds the residual query into a single narrow FP4 MMA and integrates seamlessly with paged KV caches (Kwon et al., 2023) via a device-side control kernel to reduce metadata overhead.This paper makes the following contributions:
•Accuracy-preserving FP4 KV quantization algorithm. We propose a microscaling FP4 KV quantization recipe that stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV in average accuracy with NVFP4 (within 1 point with MXFP4) across challenging long-context and reasoning benchmarks, outperforming FP8 KV and prior 4-bit methods, and generalizes across dense and MoE models up to 770B with GQA and MLA attention. In RL post-training rollouts, it closely tracks BF16 KV accuracy, avoiding the degradation of standard NVFP4.
•Fast native FP4 decoding kernels. Our native FP4 attention kernels keep the accuracy-recipe overhead within 4% and achieve up to 2.99× and 4.01× speedups over BF16 KV at 128K context on B300 and RTX PRO 5000, outperforming TRT-LLM-NVFP4, FlashInfer-XQA-NVFP4, and BitDecoding.
•High end-to-end serving efficiency. In end-to-end serving, BitDecoding-FP4 shrinks KV cache memory by up to 3.5×, cuts decoding latency by up to 1.81×, and delivers 2.4–3.0× higher peak throughput than BF16 KV at 64K–128K contexts, matching or exceeding TRT-LLM-NVFP4.
2Background and Motivation

Microscaling FP4 formats.
Microscaling formats (Rouhani et al., 2023) partition an input tensor x into contiguous blocks xb∈ℝB of size B, storing each block as B low-bit quantized elements x^b together with a single shared scalar scale sb. For 4-bit floating-point (FP4), each quantized element takes values from the E2M1 grid 𝒢E2M1={0,±0.5,±1,±1.5,±2,±3,±4,±6}. Given a block xb, the block quantizer ϕ⁡(xb)=(sb,x^b) computessb=maxi⁡|xb,i|6,x^b=roundE2M1​(xb/sb),(1)where maxi⁡|xb,i| is the maximum absolute value in xb and roundE2M1​(⋅) rounds each element to its nearest value in 𝒢E2M1, mapping the block’s largest magnitude to 6 (the maximum representable E2M1 value). Collecting (sb,x^b) across all blocks yields the quantized tensor ϕ⁡(x)=(s,x^). Dequantization multiplies the scales back, ϕ−1​(s,x^)=s⊙x^, where ⊙ broadcasts each block scale sb across the B elements of x^b, and we write Q⁡(x)=ϕ−1​(ϕ⁡(x)) for the quantize–dequantize round trip. NVFP4 uses block size B=16 with an 8-bit E4M3 scale sb, whereas MXFP4 uses B=32 with a power-of-two E8M0 scale, so sb is rounded to a power of two. Both formats natively carry fine-grained scales over 16 or 32 elements to reduce rounding error, and their E2M1 grid, which is densest near zero, fits bell-shaped tensor distributions better than the evenly spaced INT4 grid.
Accuracy drops in FP4 KV cache decoding.
With adaptive scale selection and rotation, microscaling FP4 now quantizes weights and activations accurately (Cook et al., 2025; Egiazarian et al., 2026), but the KV cache remains a gap. TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA, 2025d) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026b) store the KV cache in NVFP4 with the standard quantizer of Eq. 1. In our evaluation, TRT-LLM-NVFP4 loses 8.5 average points against BF16 KV on Qwen3-4B (Table 1). Native FP4 attention methods such as SageAttention3 (Zhang et al., 2025b) and Attn-QAT (Zhang et al., 2026) do not close this gap either: they target prefill and diffusion workloads, which quantize BF16 queries, keys, and values on the fly within each call, rather than decoding from a low-precision KV cache.Figure 2:Dequantization overhead of FlashInfer-XQA (Ye et al., 2025) kernel with NVFP4 KV Cache.
(a)Qwen3-4B
(b)Qwen3-30B-A3B

Pushing performance limits via native FP4 execution.
Most low-bit KV cache kernels dequantize the cache to BF16 (Lin et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Du et al., 2026) or FP8 (NVIDIA, 2025d) on CUDA cores before each attention matrix multiplication, leaving Tensor Cores underutilized: for an NVFP4 cache, dequantization takes 7–21% of FlashInfer-XQA’s decode kernel time at 128K context (Figure 2). NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (e.g., B300, RTX PRO 5000, and RTX 5090) remove this step with fifth-generation Tensor Cores that natively multiply block-scaled NVFP4 and MXFP4 operands (NVIDIA, 2025c) at 2–3× the throughput of FP8, consuming the E2M1 elements and block scales directly as FP4MM⁡(x^,sx,y^,sy). For attention execution, given a query q∈ℝd and cached K,V∈ℝN×d (with token rows ki,vi∈ℝd), decoding computes attention scores (logits) S=γ​q​K⊤ with per-token logit Si=γ​q⊤​ki (γ=log2⁡e/d), probabilities P=softmax⁡(S) via online softmax (Milakov and Gimelshein, 2018; Dao et al., 2022), and output o=P​V; native FP4 attention (Zhang et al., 2025b) quantizes all four operands into microscaling FP4 to execute both products via https://t.co/sZGcuUi5VE this work, we build upon the Tensor Core-aware KV layout and mixed-precision buffer of BitDecoding (Du et al., 2026), and focus on an accurate microscaling FP4 KV quantization algorithm (Section 3) and native FP4 Tensor Core kernels tailored to Blackwell GPUs (Section 4).
3FP4 KV Quantization Algorithm
In this section, we present the BitDecoding-FP4 decoding algorithm in Algorithm 1, where both attention matrix multiplications run natively on FP4 Tensor Cores and our algorithmic modifications over standard FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) are highlighted. In the following subsections, we analyze the quantization error of each operand under microscaling FP4 and detail our corresponding techniques.

3.1Dual-Residual Query Quantization

Logit error from query quantization.
Native FP4 Attention requires the quantization of both query and keys. Writing x~=Q⁡(x) for a quantized tensor and δx=x~−x for its error, the resulting logit error S~i−Si, up to the constant factor γ, decomposes into two terms:q~⊤​k~i−q⊤​ki=q~⊤​δki⏟key error+δq⊤​ki⏟query error.(2)The attention output is highly sensitive to the logit error, as the softmax turns a small logit perturbation into a shift of the attention distribution (Hooper et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025). While the large quantization error brought by key outliers has been widely reported (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026), we observe that query quantization also presents a challenge to attention accuracy. Figure 3 confirms this by splitting the logit error into its key and query terms for different query formats, showing that quantizing the query is not a second-order effect. With NVFP4 keys, the NVFP4 query contributes 60% of the logit error, more than the keys themselves.
Dual-residual quantization.
To reduce this accuracy loss, we propose Dual-Residual Query Quantization, which represents the query as the sum of two FP4 tensors. The first term is the ordinary quantized query; the second term quantizes what the first term left behind:q≈s(1)⊙q^(1)⏟q(1)=Q⁡(q)+s(2)⊙q^(2)⏟q(2)=Q⁡(q−q(1)).(3)where s(1) and s(2) are two separate sets of block scales (Eq. 1), computed from the query q and from the residual q−q(1), respectively. The query error in Eq. 2 shrinks from δq to the residual’s own rounding error q−q(1)−q(2). Section 4.2 explains how the kernel computes the logits from the two terms.Empirical results. We find that microscaling FP4 represents the residual query well: with NVFP4 keys, the dual-residual query shrinks the query term from 60% to only 1% of the logit error (Figure 3). It also outperforms smoothing Q (Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025b), which still leaves 20% of the error to the query with a mean over the GQA heads and 42% with a mean over earlier tokens (Appendix D). With MXFP4 keys, the dual-residual query likewise leaves 1%, whereas an MXFP8 query, which current Tensor Cores natively accept against MXFP4 keys, still leaves 5%.
3.2Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling

Scaling underflow for P.
We analyzed and observed that NVFP4 quantization of the softmax probabilities causes a large accuracy loss due to scaling underflow, especially in long-context decoding. Since online softmax computes pi=2Si−m from each token’s logit Si and the running maximum logit m, almost every microscaling block along the sequence has a tiny maximum, max⁡(pb)≪1. The scales of these blocks, sb=max⁡(pb)/6, when below 2−10, fall off the bottom of the E4M3 scaling range. On long reasoning traces, we observe that nearly 90% of blocks have max⁡(pb)<6⋅2−10 and get sb=0 (Figure 4(a)), which means that those tokens are never considered because their blocks are always zero, especially hurting the retrieval nature of long contexts.

"arXiv:2611.12825v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvACTl] 09 Nov 2026
MaxIM: Maximally Informative Incremental Summarization via Reinforcement Learning
Jihwan JeongGoogle ResearchGuy TennenholtzWork done while at Google.NoetiveYinlam ChowGoogle DeepMind{jihwanjeong, yinlamchow, cwhsu, cboutilier}@google.com, guytenn@gmail.comChih-Wei HsuGoogle ResearchCraig BoutilierGoogle ResearchAbstract
AI systems must often maintain bounded memory of unbounded interaction histories. However, optimizing the memory representation, and its updates, for downstream task utility is difficult for standard reinforcement learning (RL) due to severe credit assignment bottlenecks induced by sparse, delayed rewards. We introduce MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a framework that formulates incremental summarization as a capacity-constrained, information-theoretic reward-shaping problem. Grounded in value suboptimality bounds, we show that bounding sequential information loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant targets, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. We introduce a recursive consistency condition to ensure summaries are grounded by maximizing mutual information (MI) with the observed history. We mitigate credit assignment issues with a parameterized asymmetric critic that computes step-wise variational MI bounds for dense reward shaping. Empirical evaluation on long-horizon scientific reading and multi-turn dialogue benchmarks shows that MaxIM outperforms RL, supervised fine-tuning, and prompt-focused baselines on factual grounding, comprehensive autorater metrics, and downstream task utility across strict token budgets and extended horizons, without the need for expensive human preference labels.
1Introduction
A critical challenge facing AI agents in continuous, streaming environments—from real-time personalization [1, 2] to long-horizon dialogue [3, 4]—is the inability to retain unbounded context. Despite the expanded context windows of modern large language models (LLMs), processing ever-growing interaction logs frequently degrades reasoning performance due to “lost in the middle” phenomena [5]. While heuristic memory buffers (e.g., MemGPT [6]) and RL-based memory models (e.g., MemAgent [7], Mem-α [8]) offer practical mechanisms for context management, agents ultimately need rigorous methods to actively compress these streams into a fixed-capacity working memory.We assume a trainable history/context summarization policy manages this bounded memory state, while a separate, frozen action agent uses it to choose how to act in the environment. In this setting, the objective of a memory system is to maximize downstream task utility, Rtask. In principle, optimizing a summarizer using reinforcement learning (RL) on Rtask yields an optimal compression strategy. However, in long-horizon settings, task rewards are notoriously sparse and delayed, inducing extreme credit assignment failures in RL—the policy receives insufficiently granular feedback to learn which observation-stream features are predictive of task success. Conversely, optimizing for surface-level text reconstruction [9, 10] discards deeper latent intents needed for effective future inference.Figure 1:The MaxIM framework. Streaming Inference (Solid Lines): A trained actor policy incrementally compresses prior summaries zt−1 and incoming observations ot into a bounded memory zt. This memory, alongside recent observations, provides the context for a frozen downstream agent interacting with the environment with zero critic calls at test time. Asymmetric Training (Dotted Lines): During training, a pretrained critic qϕ evaluates the actor’s summary using oracle context Yt and the immediate history (zt−1,ot). It computes dense, information-theoretic shaping rewards (predictive sufficiency and recursive consistency) that step-wise guide the policy, bypassing the credit assignment bottleneck of the sparse terminal task reward Rtask.
To bridge this gap, we develop MaxIM (Maximally Informative Incremental Memory), a novel RL framework that addresses credit assignment with dense information-theoretic reward shaping. Leveraging bounds from state abstraction theory, we show that the performance gap induced by constrained memory is bounded by sequential information loss. We show that bounding this loss motivates maximizing the predictive log-likelihood of future, task-relevant target variables Yt, a variational lower bound on predictive sufficiency. However, optimizing an LLM purely for future prediction can induce severe hallucinations (i.e., fabricating plausible-sounding text that aligns with the task/target, but is disconnected from actual observations). To prevent this, we derive a recursive consistency regularizer that maximizes the mutual information (MI) with the immediate history, substantially suppressing ungrounded https://t.co/OPwkoU1mmh optimize this dual-objective, MaxIM employs RL with asymmetric context (see Figure 1). We leverage synthetic datasets to train a parameterized critic using supervised cross-entropy minimization, which computes step-wise baseline-normalized variational predictive likelihood (VPL) bounds [11], thus providing dense shaping rewards to the policy. We update the policy using standard policy gradient methods equipped with a backward-discounted reward-to-go to account for temporal error accumulation, while gradually annealing the shaping weight to ensure that late-stage training directly optimizes downstream task utility.Our contributions are: (1) We develop MaxIM, a principled RL framework for capacity-constrained generative memory that solves the sparse credit assignment bottleneck via dense information-theoretic reward shaping. (2) We link value suboptimality bounds to sequential information loss across both static and dynamic partially observable environments, deriving two complementary regularizers: predictive sufficiency and recursive consistency. (3) We offer an effective training architecture using scalable synthetic data generation and a unified asymmetric critic to compute calibrated variational lower bounds, obviating the need for human preference labels. (4) We demonstrate MaxIM’s efficacy on diverse benchmarks—a dynamic multi-turn user simulator and a novel arXiv scientific reading task—achieving superior factual grounding, token-budget Pareto efficiency, and task success.
2Related Work

Incremental Summarization and Memory Buffers.
Traditional summarization processes entire documents to generate static outputs [12, 13], whereas incremental summarization recursively updates a summary as streaming information arrives [14]. While early text streaming systems relied on clustering algorithms [15], modern neural approaches exploit structural representations (e.g., JSON states) for incremental updates [10]. A parallel line of work compresses long contexts in continuous space—including learned soft-prompt or embedding compression [16, 17, 18] and optimal-transport token-merging or KV-cache compression. These methods require either retraining the downstream model to consume continuous latents or white-box access to internal model activations. By contrast, we maintain a discrete, human-readable text memory under a token budget K, allowing it to interface directly with any frozen black-box agent. Recently, sophisticated memory buffer methods have emerged to manage unbounded LLM contexts. The closest analogs to our setup are memory systems such as MemGPT [6], Mem-α [8], and MemAgent [7]. While MemGPT and Mem-α focus on tool-calling, MemAgent learns an explicit, generative memory update policy using RL, as we do. However, these methods rely on sparse task rewards which can exacerbate hallucination and historical drift due to credit assignment failures. MaxIM builds on this foundation by introducing theoretically derived, dense MI regularizers that explicitly guide the retention of task-relevant information.
Preference Modeling and Information-Theoretic Shaping.
Modern alignment techniques like RLHF [19, 20] and RLAIF [21, 22] typically train heuristic reward models on pairwise rankings using the Bradley-Terry model [23]. While successful for general alignment, these scalar models lack formal guarantees w.r.t. preserving task-critical information and struggle with long-horizon credit assignment. While MaxIM is similar to RLAIF in its use of an oracle AI for offline data generation, we depart from preference-based rewards. Instead, we frame context compression as a reward shaping problem [24]. Specifically, by training a critic to compute calibrated VPL bounds, MaxIM provides dense, step-by-step information-theoretic rewards. This directly optimizes rigorous MI lower bounds, promoting predictive sufficiency and factual grounding without the theoretical liabilities of standard preference approximations.
RL with Asymmetric Context.
RL with asymmetric context (or privileged information) trains policies using a critic that has access to oracle information unavailable to the actor [25, 26]. Widely used in robotics to train student policies with expert teachers, we adapt it to LLM memory. By treating future text or latent intents as “oracle hindsight context,” we compute dense information-theoretic rewards that shape the LLM’s summary update policy without expensive human labels.
3Background

3.1Capacity-Constrained Memory and Sparse Rewards

Incremental Summarization.
We formalize the environment as a sequential interaction stream. An agent (or actor) engages with an environment, generating actions at∈𝒜 given a continuous stream of observations ot∈Ω. Optimal decision making generally requires conditioning on the current history Ht=(o1,a1,…,at−1,ot). Maintaining Ht indefinitely is computationally intractable for LLMs due to their finite context windows, hence, the agent adopts a summarizer policy πθ​(zt∣zt−1,at−1,ot) that incrementally updates a textual summary zt∈⋃k=1K𝒱k, where 𝒱 is the LLM vocabulary and K is a maximum token budget. The agent’s policy conditions its action choice solely on the capacity-constrained working memory zt and the current observation ot to select its next action at.11We assume the agent conditions on memory and the latest observation, though it can use the last k observations if compute and context permit. We assume the agent is fixed/frozen and focus on training the summarizer for optimal performance.
Sparse Rewards and Regularized MDPs.
The standard RL objective for optimizing policies maximizes expected cumulative task reward: J⁡(θ)=𝔼πθ​[∑tγt​Rtask,t]. However, in long-horizon settings, Rtask can be exceptionally sparse (e.g., evaluated only at the end of a multi-turn dialogue or after reading a full document). This sparsity makes RL challenging due to credit assignment failures. While classic reward shaping [24] injects dense signals without altering the optimal policy via potential functions, this is insufficient in our capacity-constrained setting. Instead, we alter the objective to form a regularized Markov decision process (MDP) [27]. By injecting dense, step-wise information-theoretic auxiliary rewards, we explicitly constrain the policy’s exploration manifold, guiding it to find an effective bounded-memory policy rather than the theoretically infeasible unconstrained optimal (which would require unbounded memory).
A Unified POMDP Formulation.
While our sequence compression formulation applies broadly, our framework models the interaction stream as a partially observable MDP (POMDP). This treats summary zt as a textual belief state tracking an unobservable latent state st∈𝒮. Crucially, this interpretation gracefully accommodates diverse streaming models, such as:
Dynamic Latent States (e.g., User Simulation): In multi-turn interactions, a user’s underlying persona, intent, or mood acts as a dynamic latent state st that evolves sequentially. The summary zt tracks this intent to guide the agent’s conversational responses.
Static Latent States and Active Perception (e.g., Goal-directed reading): For tasks like reading a scientific paper to answer eventual questions, the environment state (i.e., full document semantics and golden target answers) is static. However, with bounded context, it becomes fundamentally partially observable. Intermediate actions (e.g., reading the next text chunk) are pure sensing actions, while the summary zt serves as the belief state, accumulating the necessary sufficient statistics from the observations to resolve the unobserved target variables (questions) at the terminal step. By viewing both settings through this lens, we bridge incremental summarization and classical belief tracking, and thus establish formal value suboptimality bounds (see Section 4).
3.2Mutual Information and Representation Learning

Estimating Mutual Information.
Mutual information (MI), denoted I⁡(X,Y) and defined as I⁡(X,Y)=𝔼P⁡(x,y)​[log⁡P⁡(x,y)P⁡(x)​P​(y)], measures the reduction in uncertainty about a random variable Y given knowledge of X. Estimating MI in high-dimensional continuous or discrete spaces is difficult. One prevalent approach in representation learning, contrastive predictive coding (CPC), uses the InfoNCE loss [28]. While successfully applied to learning continuous embeddings, InfoNCE has been proven to be strictly upper-bounded by log⁡N, where N is the batch size [29]. This bound saturates rapidly when modeling high-entropy distributions like autoregressive text generation, limiting its utility as a metric for unbounded optimization.
Variational Bounds.
To overcome this log⁡N limitation, variational approximations based on f-divergences are often adopted, such as the NWJ [30] or SMILE [31] estimators. However, these estimators are known to suffer from high variance, numerical instability, and extreme hyperparameter sensitivity, particularly when the true MI is large [32]. Because of this, we focus on the VPL bound [11]. By introducing a parameterized variational distribution qϕ​(Y∣X), we leverage the non-negativity of KL divergence to establish a theoretically sound lower bound:I⁡(X,Y)≥H⁡(Y)+𝔼P⁡(x,y)​[log⁡qϕ​(y∣x)].(1)In standard representation learning, maximizing this log-likelihood maximizes I⁡(X,Y) when the marginal entropy H⁡(Y) is constant. In closed-loop POMDPs, the agent’s actions influence future states, causing H⁡(Yt) to become weakly policy-dependent. However, as we prove in Section 4, our framework circumvents this dependency: maximizing predictive log-likelihood directly bounds conditional entropy H⁡(Yt∣zt), which bounds the sequential information loss regardless of the marginal H⁡(Yt). This provides a tractable, theoretically rigorous, low-variance surrogate objective that scales naturally to modern LLMs.
4Methodology: The MaxIM Framework
We frame capacity-constrained incremental summarization as a task of information-theoretic reward shaping. Our objective is to learn a summarizer update policy πθ that dynamically creates and maintains a working memory zt, bounded by a strict token limit K, to maximize downstream task utility Rtask. Crucially, πθ is solely responsible for memory management; a separate, frozen action agent (e.g., a conversational assistant or a question-answering module) conditions on this memory zt to act within the environment. Because Rtask is often sparse and delayed in long-horizon streams (e.g., assessed only at the terminal turn T), standard RL struggles with credit assignment. Our goal is to derive principled, dense shaping rewards that offer step-by-step auxiliary guidance through the optimization landscape.
4.1Value Suboptimality and Predictive Sufficiency
Maintaining the full observation history Ht=(Ht−1,at−1,ot) is computationally intractable in streaming environments, forcing systems to compress Ht into a bounded summary zt. To quantify the impact of this compression on downstream task utility, we frame the sequential interaction as a POMDP, treating zt as a capacity-constrained Markovian state abstraction [33, 34]. CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
Peter BelcakGreg HeinrichSaurav MuralidharanShizhe DiaoPavlo MolchanovAbstract
Abstract. Large language models re-invent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.Links: Lab | Project Moonshot: Local Frontier Intelligence
1Introduction
Language models solve every problem from scratch, no matter how common. However, many of their solutions apply not just to the exact problems posed but extend to entire classes of problems in which the individual problem instances vary in their phrasing or some of their parameters. Table 1 illustrates this on an example drawn from a popular mathematical benchmark.OriginalRephrasedReparameterizedQuestionHow many positive whole-number divisors does 196 have?Find how many positive integers evenly divide https://t.co/i254YCqTp1 many positive whole-number divisors does 144 have?ReasoningI need to find the prime factorisation of 196 first. 196=4×49=22×72.
For a number with prime factorisation p1a1×p2a2×⋯, the number of divisors is (a1+1)(a2+1)⋯.
For 196=22×72: (2+1)​(2+1)=3×3=𝟗.I need to find the prime factorisation of 144 first. 144=16×9=24×32.
For a number with prime factorisation p1a1×p2a2×⋯, the number of divisors is (a1+1)(a2+1)⋯.
For 144=24×32: (4+1)​(2+1)=5×3=𝟏𝟓.Table 1:A MATH-500 problem, its rephrasing while keeping all the parameters the same, its reparametrization while keeping the phrasing the same, and the corresponding reasoning traces. The rephrased variant changes only the wording; the reparameterized variant substitutes the numerical parameter and adjusts the arithmetic accordingly. Note how neither the rephrasing nor the reparametrization change even a single word in the reasoning steps leading to the final answer, not to mention their substance.
AI agents and AI-enabled software more broadly often rely on repetitive queries to LLMs featuring the same instructions and plans but different payloads. The LLMs comprehending the same prompts and subsequently reasoning through their tasks from scratch for each new query often results in a significant amount of work being done repeatedly across separate inference instances.System-level caching (SLC) methods aim to address such inefficiencies by recognizing repetitive patterns in LM conversations and caching them at the level of the serving system as a whole rather than within any single inference instance. Maintained at the system level, an SLC’s entries are shared across all of the system’s inference instances and remain reusable beyond the instance in which they were born. SLC methods usually bring one or more of the following benefits:
•Cost and latency reduction. SLC methods can reduce the cost and/or the latency of LLM calls by re-using partial or complete results of earlier LLM calls.
•Improved correctness. SLCs can be reviewed asynchronously by humans or a committee of judge agents to ensure that the responses or steps of the most popular queries are correct.
•Improved explainability or interpretability. SLCs can be inspected by humans to understand the reasoning process and the final answer or result, providing explanation or at the very least an interpretation of responses to popular queries.When choosing or designing an SLC method, the following considerations are important:
•Local robustness. How well does the SLC method cover the class of queries it is supposed to cover? How robust is the SLC method to small perturbations of the queries?
•Correctness upon hit. If the cache is hit, is the result correct? How much confidence can one have in the correctness of the cached result given a hit from the query neighbourhood it covers?
•Explainability or interpretability. How much can one learn by inspecting the caches? How good are the guarantees of correctness provided by the cache entries? Can they be inspected by an authority (e.g., a regulatory body) to provide a guarantee on behavior?
•Cost. How expensive is it to build, maintain, and use the SLC?Existing work on SLC falls into two broad categories:
•Monolithic caching. Methods such as ephemeral prefix caching [1], programmatic conversation caching [2, 3], and semantic query matching [4] look up transcripts of previous conversations on the basis of input prefix overlaps, programmatically supplied conversation IDs, and semantic similarities between different queries. They store entire conversations and their corresponding intermediate generation states (e.g., KV caches or Mamba hidden states) and aim to re-use the largest possible contiguous portion of the query’s generation states wherever possible. Monolithic caches are usually not robust to even the slightest perturbations of the conversation, and when they are (e.g., when employing semantic similarity search), it is often at the expense of their correctness. Monolithic caches of responses can be inspected to guarantee absolute correctness. They are usually compute-cheap to build, maintain, and use but are memory- and bandwidth-expensive to maintain and use.
•Modular caching. Instead of storing the entire conversational transcripts and their generation artifacts, modular SLC methods first perform a mechanical form of decomposition of the existing contexts and their generation states or a distillation of the context into critical logical steps [5, 6, 7]. Later, when encountering an apparently similar problem, the decomposed artifacts are re-supplied to the language model to accelerate their reasoning process. Only parts of the response are cached, and even in the case of a perfect cache hit, a full new generation (though accelerated) of the response is still required. This makes their coverage more robust to parametric perturbations of the inputs but makes it impossible to guarantee correctness upon review. Modular caches sometimes offer interpretable insights into the reasoning process of the underlying models. They are considerably more compute-expensive to build and use than monolithic caches but tend to be more memory- and bandwidth-efficient to maintain and use.We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a (see below) hybrid SLC method that produces agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) that are robust in coverage, can be asynchronously ensured to be correct, are fully explainable, and are cheap to build, maintain, and use. We call them agentic reasoning caches because their elements are small, specialized fractional agents that can be re-used on new parameters. Our approach rests on two observations:
O1Once a particular problem has been reasoned through and the solution has been found, the execution of the solution – the computation or data manipulation behind the problem – can be performed with little involvement from language models. In other words, the search for a solution can be decoupled from the execution of the solution found.
O2Much of LM’s reasoning about a particular problem instance can be reused for a set of problems extending beyond the singleton instance.Leveraging Observation O1, we choose to convert LM conversation transcripts to code, and allow that code to make use of only small language models to perform semantic similarity search and elementary natural language processing tasks such as value extraction, format conversion, classification, or summarization, and only where needed. Leveraging Observation O2, we choose to parametrize the code in a way that allows it to be re-used for all problems that are equirational to the problem solved in the original transcript (i.e., can be solved using the same reasoning). Further, we choose to produce code in such a manner that does not rely on fixed variable, parameter, and function names but on their natural language descriptions and examples, thus allowing for a liberal re-use of all logical components of previously cached logic in all semantically equivalent scenarios, no matter how phrased, structured, or parameterized.Agentic reasoning caching is a hybrid of monolithic and modular SLC because it decomposes the logic of an LLM conversation into a network of modules – semantic functions – that can be re-used individually and also provides their composition into a single function that can be used to solve the problem cached. Because of the semantic functions’ wide parametrization, ARCs are robust to logically valid parametric perturbations of the problem. Since every ARC entry is stored as code, ARCs are fully explainable and correctible upon human or AI inspection. Since ARCs are stored as code using only SLMs, they are cheap to maintain and use since they rely mostly on CPU execution. They are further relatively cheap to build, coming at 12-84x the cost of the original reasoning.Figure 1:Gated use of an agentic reasoning cache. The cache is tried first; on a miss or error, the request falls through to the full LLM.
def serve(request):try:result = cache.use(request)if result is not False:return resultexcept CacheInvocationError:passreturn llm(request)Agentic reasoning caching is particularly suitable for agentic systems that repeatedly use the same prompts with variable payloads. In an agentic system, using an ARC can be attempted before forwarding the request to the cloud LLM, allowing for a significant reduction in the latency and cost in the case of a cache hit. Owing to their reliance on simple CPU execution and SLMs, agentic reasoning caches are so resource-efficient that they can be brought to edge devices, reducing the cost further. Figure 1 briefly illustrates the gated use of an agentic reasoning cache in an AI system where the cache re-use is attempted before forwarding the request to the full LLM.Our contributions are:
C1The introduction of agentic reasoning caching, a hybrid SLC method that is robust in its coverage, can be asynchronously ensured to be correct by human or AI inspection, is fully explainable, and is cheap to build, maintain, and use.
C2The evaluation of agentic reasoning caching on a range of challenging mathematical and science benchmarks, including its success rates, correctness, robustness, and cost-saving capabilities.
C3A brief discussion of the intended placement and implications of this work.Our long-term goal is to bring ARC to real production agents to help lower their cost. In this initial, exploratory work, we deliberately focus on the hardest case: rather than agentic workloads of varied difficulty, we test whether ARCs can match frontier-level model performance on difficult mathematical and scientific benchmarks that are commonly used to measure intelligence. Succeeding at that (as we show we do) indicates that the method is not capped by the ability of models to produce these small ARCs, and that, by extension, the broader class of agentic tasks currently driven by frontier-level models is plausibly cacheable as well.
2Agentic reasoning caching
Let 𝒮,ℬ,𝒯 be the source, builder, and target language model, respectively, and 𝒜 be an answering oracle that answers all queries correctly. Here, the source 𝒮 is the capable, expensive model whose intelligence we aim to cache; the builder ℬ is the model that analyzes 𝒮’s reasoning transcripts and constructs cache entries; and the target 𝒯 is the small, cost-efficient model on which caches are to execute at inference time. Additionally, in some places we make use of LM judges 𝒥, which are simply language models tasked with verifying the correctness and faithfulness of intermediate and final outputs throughout construction and evaluation. Let q(∙1,∙2,…,∙n) be a query template with n parameters.Let q⁡(o) be a query instance submitted for caching with o being a specific value vector for q’s parameters.Assume that 𝒜⁡(q⁡(o)) exists, meaning that q⁡(o) is solvable. Observe that there exists a set of parameter vectors Π such that for all π∈Π, q⁡(π) is equirational to q⁡(o). This is because at the very least, q⁡(o) is equirational to itself.Agentic reasoning caching is based on the following two assumptions:A1For every q⁡(o) that is solvable there exists a program p(∙1,∙2,…,∙n) with access to an SLM such that p⁡(π)=𝒜⁡(q⁡(π)) for all π∈Π.
A2p(∙1,∙2,…,∙n) can be constructed by ℬ from knowing q⁡(o) and 𝒮⁡(q⁡(o)).Assumption A1 effectively amounts to the belief that every solvable problem is solvable with a combination of code and a small language model in a way that extends to all equirational variants of the problem. Assumption A2 expresses the belief that it is possible to encode into p by some language model ℬ the intelligence in 𝒮 required to solve q⁡(o) and its equirational variants using q⁡(o) and its output under 𝒮 as starting points.Agentic reasoning caching is the embodiment of the above assumptions. Implementing Assumption A1, we ask the builder model to analyze source model conversation transcripts to be cached to find which parts (together with their ranges of validity) of their inputs can be varied without requiring substantive changes to the reasoning. Further implementing Assumption A2, we ask the builder model to comprehend the source transcript and construct a program that can solve the problem posed in the original query considering the above-found input parts as parameters that can be varied. To ensure maximal robustness and cache coverage, we insist that the program is a rich composition of independently invokable units representing logical steps that constitute the reasoning process, which we call semantic functions. An agentic reasoning cache is then a set of semantic functions combined with a many-to-one map of problem instances to the natural language descriptions of the semantic functions that can solve the respective instances.The remainder of this section describes the semantic functions that constitute programs p (Section 2.1) and the cache construction (Section 2.2.1) and invocation (Section 2.2.2) processes.
2.1Semantic functions
A semantic function is an executable abstraction representing one logical step of the source reasoning trace, designed to be maximally reusable across semantically equivalent contexts. They are the matter of which agentic reasoning caching is made up. In our implementation, it is simply a Python callable that takes a Context object and returns a dictionary mapping natural-language descriptions to values:f:Context⟶dict[str, Any].Unlike conventional functions whose inputs, outputs, and callees are referenced by fixed identifiers, semantic functions reference everything by natural-language descriptions and examples. This enables semantic discovery: a caller need not know the callee’s name, only a description of what it does, and a callee need not know the names of its inputs, only their descriptions. This design allows any component of a previously cached computation to be reused in any semantically equivalent scenario regardless of how it is phrased or structured (Figure 2). Further, if a change (such as a generalization introducing new parameter) is made to a dependency semantic function, none of its callers need to be updated. Instead, its new, generalized description will open it to a larger set of callers, again without affecting its past callers as long as the new description semantically entails the old one.
Runtime primitives.
Semantic functions are designed to use a small set of runtime primitives that mediate all data flow and computation:
•load(ctx, query): retrieve a value from the layered context memory via vector similarity search. An optional d_type parameter triggers type coercion on the retrieved value.
•do(ctx, query, payloads): discover and invoke another semantic function by natural-language description. Pushes an isolated memory layer pre-populated with the given payloads, executes the matched function, and returns its output dictionary.
•narrate(ctx, message): record a human-readable reasoning step in the narration trace, providing a running explanation of the computation for later inspection.
•lm(ctx, prompt): query the target model 𝒯 for an elementary natural-language processing task such as classification, summarization, or short-form generation.
•extract(ctx, text, prompt): use 𝒯 to perform verbatim value extraction from a piece of text. Supports d_type for type coercion on the extracted value.
•convert(ctx, value, type) / smart_convert(ctx, text, type): multi-tier type coercion. Programmatic conversion is attempted first; if it fails, smart_convert asks 𝒯 to rewrite the value into a Python literal that is then validated by ast.literal_eval().
•invoke_tool(ctx, name, args): call a registered external tool (e.g., terminal or a web search API), enabling semantic functions to integrate with tool-augmented pipelines.
Type safety.
Because values flow between functions through semantic search rather than typed variable bindings, type coercion is critical. Both load and extract accept an optional d_type parameter that coerces the retrieved or extracted value to the desired Python type. When direct coercion fails, smart_convert invokes 𝒯 to rewrite the value into a Python literal, which is then parsed via ast.literal_eval() to ensure syntactic validity and type correctness.
Composition via do and load.
Semantic functions are composed into networks through the do() primitive. The do() primitive invokes a semantic function by describing its intention imperatively in natural language and passing parameters annotated by their natural language descriptions. A caller passes described parameter values into do(), which pushes a fresh, isolated memory layer onto the context stack, populates it with the payloads, and dispatches to the callee found by semantic search over the function registry. The callee accesses its inputs via load() and stores its outputs into the same layer. Upon return, the caller retrieves results from the callee’s output dictionary with load(result, query). This mechanism enables hierarchical decomposition: a root function can delegate to arbitrarily nested sub-functions based on its intention rather than their named identities, with each sub-function operating in its own scope while sharing the underlying context stack. See Figure 5 in Appendix A for a complete cache entry illustrating these primitives on an ideal gas law problem from SciBench.
Context and memory model.
The Context object maintains a stack of memory layers, each backed by a CPU-powered vector store using a small semantic embedding model. When load() is called, it searches the layers top-down, returning the best match from the most local scope. Each invocation of do() pushes a new layer and pops it upon completion, providing natural scoping that prevents unintended interference between sibling calls.

Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving
Journal: Knowledge-Based SystemsGabriel Souza Baggio, Gabriel Machado LunardiFederal University of Santa Maria, Roraima Avenue, 1000, Santa Maria, 97105-800, Rio Grande do Sul, BrazilGuilherme Medeiros Machado, Subhankar Maity, Faiza BelbachirLyRIDS lab, ECE Engineering School, 10 Rue Sextius Michel, Paris, 75015, Île-de-France, FranceJosé Palazzo Moreira de OliveiraFederal University of Rio Grande do Sul, Informatics Institute, Bento Gonçalves Avenue, 9500, Porto Alegre, 91501-970, Rio Grande do Sul, BrazilAbstract
Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.Retrieval-Augmented Generation , Large Language Models , Code Generation , Programming Problems , Information RetrievalKeywords:

1Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated proficiency in solving generic problems across various professional domains [37, 20, 38]. Although some evaluation benchmarks indicate high performance — such as on HumanEval, where GPT-4o [28] and Claude-3.5-Sonnet [3] achieved precision scores of 90% and 92%, respectively [40] —, other benchmarks show that LLMs exhibit limitations on competitive programming tasks [8, 43, 17, 39]. For instance, in the analysis by Zheng et al. [43], Claude-3.5-Sonnet achieved a 0% precision rate on medium and hard problems and only 14.1% on easy ones. In the same benchmark, even the best-performing LLMs, such as Gemini-2.5-Pro [15] and DeepSeek-R1 [9], could not solve a single hard problem.These errors typically arise due to a lack of specific contextual knowledge and a limited understanding of underlying data structures, leading to hallucinations — outputs that are syntactically invalid or logically inconsistent [24]. Under a deeper epistemological analysis, it becomes evident that Large Language Models (LLMs) operate on opinion-based trajectories—that is, on the formulation of statements not necessarily grounded in verifiable evidence, but rather derived from inferences or interpretations constructed within a limited context of knowledge. Hallucination, in this sense, may be understood as the generation of a perception or belief that, while internally coherent, does not correspond to empirical reality. In LLMs, this phenomenon arises because the model “believes” it is producing a consistent and contextually appropriate response, even though such a response lacks factual https://t.co/6AuCmHiPuB mitigate this, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [18, 13] has been proposed as a mechanism to ground the model’s outputs in relevant external knowledge by, with an Information Retrieval (IR) algorithm, retrieving contextually similar information from a structured corpus [18, 13]. This work investigates how RAG can be used to enhance the problem-solving capabilities of LLMs.The proposition for applying RAG in this context is based on two key observations. First, studies indicate that problems within competitive programming repositories often share underlying algorithmic patterns and solution structures [10, 11]. Second, the practice of providing relevant examples in the prompt (few-shot prompting) is an established technique for improving LLM performance on complex tasks [31, 25]. Based on this,the hypothesis is  that a RAG system that retrieves previously solved problems with analogous characteristics to a target problem can provide the model with relevant context and reduce https://t.co/HOLELiqhkT achieve this, we developed an Information Retrieval (IR) pipeline that employs embedding similarity with a dynamic threshold [5]. We evaluated this system on the CodeContests dataset [23], which is divided into a training set of 13,328 problems and a test set of 165 problems. In addition to the problem title and statement, each sample includes metadatdynamig programming, bitwise operations). The training split served as the knowledge base from which we retrieved similar examples to augment the LLM prompts for solving the problems in the test set. The correctness of the generated solutions was then evaluated using the CodeForces [27] judge system, allowing us to measure the impact of the retrieved context on the model’s performance.The evaluation involves three distinct prompting strategies: (i) a zero-shot baseline using only the original description, (ii) a random retrieval baseline retrieving unrelated problems from the knowledge base, and (iii) the proposed similarity-based RAG approach retrieving contextually aligned examples. Our analyses demonstrate that the similarity-based retrieval consistently outperforms both baselines, validating the hypothesis that retrieving analogous problems improves LLM reasoning on complex programming tasks. Furthermore, the Min-K membership inference results reveal that many generated code lines correspond to known training patterns, underscoring the importance of disentangling memorization effects from genuine reasoning improvements. Together, these findings provide a dual epistemic safeguard: RAG anchors outputs in external knowledge, while membership inference verifies their originality and data provenance. See Figure 1 for a graphical overview of the system architecture and execution pipeline.Figure 1:System Architecture and Execution Pipeline
The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:1.We design a RAG framework tailored to competitive programming tasks, integrating an embedding-based similarity search with an adaptive thresholding mechanism to retrieve contextually relevant problems while minimizing retrieval noise.
2.We construct a comprehensive experimental setup using the CodeContests dataset, evaluating six prominent LLMs across three prompting strategies, zero-shot, random retrieval, and RAG-based enhancement, to systematically quantify the effect of similarity-driven retrieval on code generation performance.
3.We introduce a complementary Min-K Membership Inference analysis to assess model exposure and memorization biases, providing a novel perspective on the interplay between retrieval-based augmentation and pretraining data recall.
4.We present an integrated evaluation pipeline combining RAG effectiveness and membership inference insights, offering a dual perspective on both performance improvement and epistemic grounding in competitive programming contexts.
5.Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the design of future reasoning-oriented LLMs and outline directions for extending this work to upcoming state-of-the-art models such as Gemini 3 and GPT-5.
2Related Works
Several works have investigated the ability of LLMs to solve competitive programming problems, experimenting different evaluation metrics and approaches to maximize the correctness of generated solutions [33, 32, 19, 43, 10, 17, 8].
2.1Evaluation Strategies
A main challenge in this domain is developing evaluation metrics that go beyond simple pass/fail rates and accurately reflect a model’s problem-solving skill [32]. While simply annotating the number of correctly solved problems is informative, it fails to distinguish between solving a trivial problem and solving one that challenges even the best human competitors [43].To address this gap, recent benchmarks [32, 30, 6] have adopted the Elo rating system [12], a method widely recognized for assessing the relative skill levels of players in competitive games — and is also used in CodeForces platform. In the context of competitive programming platforms, the Elo system provides a unified scale to quantify both problem difficulty and competitor skill. The difficulty rating d assigned to a problem is calibrated against the entire community of human participants; a contestant with an Elo rating of d has a 50% probability of solving this given problem [6].The Elo rating of a contestant, in turn, provides a clear measure of their standing within the competitive community [43]. For example, a rating of 1600 (an “Expert” on CodeForces) places a user in the top 11% of active participants, while a rating of 2400 (“Grandmaster”) signifies performance in the top 1%. An elite rating of 2700 indicates a skill level superior to approximately 99.9% of competitors. By framing LLM performance in this way, we can move from asking “how many” problems a model solved to “how skilled” the model is.Following this evaluation method, our study treats each LLM as a virtual contestant and calculates its equivalent Elo rating. We specifically employ Bayesian Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) Elo rating [44], a method also utilized in [43], to estimate the most probable skill level of a model given its performance.The estimation process begins with the standard Elo probability function, πi​(R), which calculates the likelihood of a model with rating R correctly solving a problem with difficulty di:πi​(R)=11+10(di−R)/400These individual probabilities are used to construct the unnormalized log-posterior function, ℒ⁡(R). This function combines the log-likelihood of the observed outcomes (yi∈{1​ for accepted,0​ for rejected}) across all N problems with a regularizing Gaussian prior on the model’s rating (with mean μ0 and variance σ02):ℒ⁡(R)=∑i=1N[yi​ln⁡πi​(R)+(1−yi)​ln⁡(1−πi​(R))]−(R−μ0)22​σ02Finally, the MAP estimate, R^MAP, is the rating R that maximizes this log-posterior function:R^MAP=arg⁡max𝑅​ℒ​(R)Since our benchmark utilizes the CodeContests dataset [23], which contains most of its problems from CodeForces, we annotated each problem’s official Elo difficulty rating. This provides a standardized metric that allows for a comparison of our results against other benchmarks (assuming they also use Elo), even when the test sets are composed of different problems.
2.2Performance Enhancement Approaches
Prior research has explored enhancing LLM performance through two main strategies: granting models access to external knowledge sources or fine-tuning them on specific datasets. For instance, augmenting models with tools like terminal and internet access has enabled systems such as o3 and o4-mini-high to achieve Elo ratings of 2706 and 2719 respectively [30]. Another strategy involves fine-tuning LLMs on competitive programming datasets to train them on problem-solving patterns, a notable example being Google’s AlphaCode [23]. Since these benchmarks also use Elo for evaluation, we used it as a common metric to assess the effectiveness of our technique in relation to these prior work.
2.3Problem Datasets
Several datasets have been proposed to benchmark the ability of LLMs to solve competitive programming problems [33, 32, 19, 43, 23]. Table 1 summarizes these datasets, detailing how many problems each contains and the time period from which they were sourced.Table 1:Summary of competitive programming datasets used for LLM evaluationDataset# ProblemsProblems’ Year(s)USACO [33]3072011-2024CodeElo [32]4082024LiveCodeBench [19]4422023-2024LiveCodeBench Pro [43]∼584Updated LivelyCodeContests [23]13,4932021
For this study, we selected the CodeContests dataset due to its extensive scale. Our central hypothesis is that retrieving similar, previously solved problems can enhance an LLM’s performance. The large repository of over 13,000 problems in CodeContests provides a sufficiently dense knowledge base, which is essential for a retrieval-based approach to effectively find analogous examples.Other benchmarks, while valuable, were less suited for our research objectives. The USACO dataset, for instance, sources its problems from a platform other than CodeForces, making it incompatible with the Elo rating system used for our evaluation. Datasets like CodeElo, LiveCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench Pro, despite their advantages of containing more recent problems and potentially having less data contamination, offer a very limited number of problems.
3Methodology
To evaluate RAG’s impact on our work, we used six well-known LLMs and a set of programming questions, each paired with a previously tested and accepted solution. These entries serve as the knowledge base for the RAG. All datasets and code used in the methodology are included in our open-source repository11https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ArtigoSBBD-C51C.
3.1Model Selection
The models utilized were chosen based on their use in prior research: DeepSeek-R1 [43, 40, 10], Gemini 2.0 Flash [43, 19, 10], Claude 3.7 Sonnet [43, 10], Qwen models [43, 19, 40, 32], GPT-4-omni [43, 19, 17, 40, 32, 10], and GPT-3.5 Turbo [33, 19]. This section provides information about the models used:Table 2:Overview of models with organization, context window and cut-off date.Full Model NameOrg.Context TokensCut-off DateDeepSeek-R1 [1]DeepSeek131KNot specifiedGemini 2.0 Flash [14]Google1 millionJune 2024Claude 3.7 Sonnet [4]Anthropic200KOctober 2024Qwen2.5-Coder-32B [2]Alibaba128KEnd of 2023GPT-4-omni [28]OpenAI128KSeptember 2023GPT-3.5 Turbo [29]OpenAI16KSeptember 2021
Another decisive factor in the model selection was the diversity in training focus and knowledge cutoff date: we included a code-specialized model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B), a model known for advanced reasoning capabilities (DeepSeek-R1), a less powerful model (GPT-3.5 Turbo), as well as general-purpose models with broader training data.
3.2Information Retrieval Algorithm
The IR algorithm retrieves similar solved problems from the database. First, each problem description in the database is transformed into a high-dimensional vector embedding using the ‘all-MiniLM-L6-v2’22https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model. These embeddings capture the semantic essence of the problems [22]. The collection of embeddings is then indexed using FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) [21], employing an ‘IndexFlatL2’ structure that computes Euclidean distances. Because the vectors are already normalized, we can compute the similarity directly from the Euclidean distance (on a 0-to-1 scale).A distinctive aspect of our IR system is its adaptive threshold mechanism, introduced by [5]. Instead of a fixed cutoff, the threshold for deeming a retrieved problem “similar enough” is dynamically adjusted based on the highest similarity score. The initial threshold used for the similarity is 70%, but if the highest similarity is strong (above 85%), the threshold becomes more stringent; if weaker (less than 75%), it relaxes, but never below the 70% minimum. Similar adaptive strategies are used in RAG to reduce noise [42], and we apply it with the same intent. As an additional measure to mitigate noise, the system is configured to return a maximum of the three most similar problems.
3.3Dataset Overview
We utilized the CodeContests dataset [23] for this study, designating its training set as the knowledge base for our RAG system and its test set for evaluation. The dataset, sourced primarily from CodeForces problems, is structured as a JSON file where each entry contains the problem’s title, its full description, input/output examples, the official CodeForces rating (when applicable), relevant thematic tags, and verified code solutions. These problems do not require a specific programming language for implementation, allowing for flexibility in the solution approaches. This section describes how we leveraged this dataset to construct our RAG pipeline and analyzes the distribution of difficulties and categories of the problems used.Of the 165 problems in the CodeContests test set, 81 had at least one similar problem found in the knowledge base by our Information Retrieval algorithm. The evaluation was therefore performed on this subset, as the remaining problems had no retrieved counterparts and would not receive any additional information from the RAG system. Furthermore, none of the problems in this evaluation set were part of the RAG’s knowledge base, ensuring a fair assessment of its generalization capabilities [18, 13, 35, 26]. Problems can be classified into one or more categories (e.g., dynamic programming, sorting, binary search), and the distribution of these thematic tags across both datasets is shown in Figure https://t.co/CQ3GfgENac better understand the difficulty distribution of the problems, we performed a classification based on their CodeForces Elo ratings. While the Elo system provides a continuous scale, we grouped the problems into three discrete categories for a better analysis: Easy, Medium, and Hard. Problems with an Elo rating between 0 and 1000 were classified as Easy, those in the range (1000, 2000] as Medium, and any problem rated above 2000 as Hard. It is worth noting that while every problem in the test set is from CodeForces, the training set (our knowledge base) also contains problems from other sources, so not all of them had the CodeForces Elo information available. Table 3 shows the distribution of these difficulty levels across the knowledge base and our filtered test dataset.📷Figure 2:Categories of the Problems from the Knowledge and Test Datasets

3.4Min-K-Based Membership Inference Analysis
To complement the RAG evaluation and assess whether any code solutions in the test set were potentially present in the training corpora of the evaluated LLMs, we implemented a Min-K Membership Inference approach [34]. This method estimates the likelihood that a given code sample was part of a model’s pretraining data, thereby quantifying exposure bias and memorization within large language models.The core intuition behind this algorithm is that language models assign systematically higher confidence to samples encountered during training compared to unseen ones. Training data typically yield higher average token probabilities (or equivalently, lower perplexities). Rather than relying on mean likelihoods, the Min-K approach focuses on the lowest K% of token log-probabilities, representing the model’s most uncertain predictions, because these regions provide stronger discriminatory signals between memorised and novel samples [34]. By analyzing the extremal uncertainty pattern rather than overall fluency, the method enhances detection precision and reduces false positives.Algorithm 1 summarizes the membership inference detection process for code snippets. Given a tokenized code sequence x=(x1,x2,…,xn), the model fθ computes the conditional log-probabilities for each token.
